title: A Performance Review With a Clear Growth Plan
script: Manager: [warmly] Ratih, this six-month review will cover results, support, and one development goal. You may ask for clarification at any point.
Ratih: Thank you. I prepared notes because review meetings make me nervous.
Manager: [thoughtful] Your completion rate improved, and client feedback says your responses are clearer and faster. The report shows the period and project types we measured.
Ratih: I am glad the new weekly planning system helped.
Manager: One area I want to understand is participation in planning meetings. You often send useful ideas afterward rather than during discussion.
Ratih: [honestly] I need time to organize my thoughts, and fast group conversations make me worry that an unfinished idea will sound careless.
Manager: That is useful context. The goal is not speaking for its own sake. We need your knowledge before decisions close.
Ratih: Could agendas include the main questions earlier?
Manager: [encouraging] Yes. I will send decision questions one day ahead where possible. You can add written input before the meeting.
Ratih: I would also like the chair to invite me on the topic I prepared, rather than expecting me to interrupt.
Manager: That is reasonable. For urgent or safety-related claims, bring evidence or say what still needs checking. We will not use an arbitrary rule such as speaking when “seventy percent sure.”
Ratih: [reflective] What would improvement look like over the next month?
Manager: Contribute to two relevant planning decisions, verbally or in writing, and record what support helped. Quality matters more than a word count.
Ratih: Can we review it after four weeks instead of waiting six months?
Manager: [warmly] Yes. I also want feedback on whether the meeting format gives everyone a fair chance to contribute.
Ratih: Then the plan addresses both my skill and the team environment.
Manager: Exactly. Development should not mean forcing one communication style on every employee.
Ratih: [determined] I will prepare for tomorrow’s agenda and add one written question this afternoon.
Manager: Good. I will send you the performance data and our agreed actions so you can correct anything I recorded inaccurately.
Ratih: [sincere] Thank you. Specific evidence and a clear follow-up make the feedback feel useful, not vague.

quiz.question: When does Ratih often send ideas?
quiz.explanation: Her knowledge arrives too late for some decisions.

quiz.question: What change will the manager make?
options: Send main decision questions earlier when possible

quiz.question: How many relevant decisions form the practice goal?
quiz.explanation: The development target is specific and modest.

quiz.question: What record will the manager send?
quiz.explanation: Ratih can check the accuracy of the review record.

quiz.question: What evidence supports Ratih’s strong performance?
options: Completion data and client feedback have improved
quiz.explanation: The praise is tied to observable work.

quiz.question: Why does Ratih stay quiet?
options: She fears her ideas are not developed enough
quiz.explanation: The barrier is confidence and meeting design.

quiz.question: Why is “speak when seventy percent sure” removed?
options: Some topics require evidence, and a percentage is unclear and arbitrary
quiz.explanation: Advice should fit risk and purpose.

quiz.question: What options will help Ratih contribute?
options: Agenda questions, preparation time, written input, and an invited speaking point
quiz.explanation: Multiple channels reduce one narrow performance demand.

quiz.question: How will progress be reviewed?
options: With examples of contributions and a follow-up meeting
Only at the next annual review
quiz.explanation: The plan uses behavior and timely support.
